title: Media Ownership
blurb: Concentration, regulation and the platforms: parliament on the press.

brief.question: What does the parliamentary record show about media ownership?
brief.answer:
The strongest and most decision-relevant finding in the record is that Labor speakers repeatedly argued that Australia already had a highly concentrated media market, dominated by Rupert Murdoch’s News Ltd and the Packer family’s Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd, and that the Howard government’s proposed changes would make concentration worse. Labor quoted figures showing News Ltd controlled two-thirds of capital city and national newspapers, almost three-quarters of Sunday newspapers, almost half of suburban newspapers and a quarter of regional newspapers, with a quarter share in Foxtel. PBL was said to reach more than half the potential television audience, publish 65 magazines, and hold major online and pay-TV interests. Against this, one Labor speaker cited research that 80 per cent of Australians opposed further media concentration, and another cited Productivity Commission findings that a proprietor’s business and editorial interests were likely to influence content and opinion. Cross-media rules introduced under the Keating government in the late 1980s were defended as preventing any one proprietor being both “queen of the screen” and “prince of print,” and as preserving at least some diversity.

The debate shifted over time through repeated attempts at legislative change: the Broadcasting Services Amendment (Media Ownership) Bill 2002, a second 2002 bill, and the 2006 bill. The government’s stated case, put by Senator Alston and others, was that ownership of media “per se is irrelevant,” that new media and the internet created a “plethora of sources,” and that separate editorial processes could protect diversity. Labor responded with evidence that most Australians still relied on traditional media—88 per cent used free-to-air television for news, 76 per cent used radio and 76 per cent used newspapers, while only 10 per cent used pay TV and 11 per cent used the internet—and that the major internet news sites were owned by the same established media players. Labor also noted that the 2002 bill initially would have allowed one proprietor to own television, newspapers and radio in one market, and that after Senate lobbying the government signalled it might settle for two of the three, which Labor said exposed the real agenda.

The sharpest disagreement was over whether ownership itself determines media content and democratic influence. Labor speakers insisted that “he who pays the piper calls the tune” and that no editorial separation test could protect the public when a proprietor can hire and fire journalists and set the ultimate direction. They rejected the idea that journalists’ independence could be separated from their employer’s commercial interests, and attacked Australian Broadcasting Authority chairman Professor David Flint for arguing ownership did not dominate content. Labor also accused the government of hypocrisy, noting that coalition backbenchers such as the member for Hinkler, the future Minister for Citizenship and Multicultural Affairs, and the Minister for Education, Science and Training had spoken strongly against concentration in the 1990s but were silent once on the front bench. The most incendiary charge came from the member for Lowe, who alleged a secret deal between Prime Minister Howard and Kerry Packer dating from 1995, called the 2006 bill a “disgraceful piece of chicanery,” and claimed it would allow PBL to use a war chest of between $4½ billion and $4¾ billion—or possibly $6 billion—to buy more casino assets and dominate media, including acquiring Fairfax.

On promises versus outcomes, the record shows the government promised safeguards, but Labor said those promises were hollow. In answer to a question from the member for Lowe, the Prime Minister said the bill would use exemptions and undertakings to maintain existing levels of locally produced news and current affairs and to require separate editorial processes. Labor dismissed this as nonsense, noting it said nothing about dominant city markets and would entrench concentration rather than protect diversity. Labor also argued that the proposed editorial separation test would create unprecedented government interference in media operations, a position criticised by the Australian Press Council and Fairfax as well as by public-interest and industry groups. Despite the government’s claims that its changes would enhance diversity, Labor concluded that the effect would be to create three huge conglomerates, allow Packer to buy Fairfax, and allow Murdoch to take a free-to-air network, leaving Australia with greater concentration, fewer independent newsrooms, and a diminished capacity for the media to hold governments accountable.

sections.question: What have MPs said about media ownership concentration in Australia?
sections.answer:
Australian parliamentarians have repeatedly warned that further media ownership concentration threatens democracy and the public interest. Labor MPs, including the member for Throsby, have argued that allowing proprietors to own television, radio, and newspapers in the same market would "attack our democracy at its very heart" and reduce diversity, competition, and consumer choice. They have cited Paul Keating's principle that media owners should be either "queens of the screen" or "princes of print," not both.

Government backbenchers have also voiced concerns. In 1995, the member for Hinkler warned of "the centralising of media control" and called for a stand against it. The member for Moreton (later Minister for Citizenship and Multicultural Affairs) said in 1996 that "diversity has all but disappeared" due to concentration, and in 2000 noted that cross-media rules were becoming redundant but owners should "exercise some real responsibility." The member for Bradfield (later Minister for Education, Science and Training) said in 1997 that his constituents would not support further concentration and that a proprietor controlling TV and newspapers in Sydney and Melbourne was "not a legacy we wish to leave upon our children." Critics have accused these frontbenchers of hypocrisy for abandoning those views once in government.

The Australian Greens have stated that Australia has "the most concentrated media ownership in the Western world" and that this is "corrosive of the fabric of Australian democracy." They have called for keeping the two-out-of-three rule as a minimum safeguard.

Specific figures cited include News Limited owning 147 newspapers, with daily and Sunday titles accounting for over 69% of total circulation, and metropolitan sales potentially reaching around 80% if Monday-to-Friday calculations are used. Kerry Stokes, proprietor of the Seven Network, admitted to a parliamentary committee that abolishing the 75% reach rule could let him "absolutely dominate" media in Western Australia, which he conceded was not in the public interest.

sections.question: What was said about the news media bargaining code and tech platforms?
sections.answer:
The news media bargaining code was repeatedly framed as a world-first Australian response to a stark bargaining power imbalance between global digital platforms—chiefly Google and Meta (Facebook)—and Australian news businesses. Speakers from the Coalition credited their government with initiating the reform in 2019 after voluntary negotiations failed, delivering the mandatory code in 2021. They claimed it produced more than 30 commercial agreements worth an estimated $250 million annually to Australian news organisations, citing deals with Seven West, Nine, Fairfax, and Junkee Media as evidence it worked. The Coalition stressed the code’s negotiate-arbitrate model, with the Treasurer designating platforms based on ACCC advice, and highlighted minimum standards like 14 days’ notice of algorithm changes and a default offer mechanism for smaller and regional publishers.

Labor acknowledged the code’s initial success but argued its design had a critical loophole: platforms could avoid obligations by removing news from their services, as Meta did briefly in Australia in 2021 and later in Canada. Labor noted Meta’s April 2024 decision not to renew commercial agreements—estimated at around $70 million a year—and its threat to drop news entirely, giving a company with enormous market power a bargaining tool. Labor’s proposed fix was a "news bargaining incentive" scheme, a market-based model with a clear preference for commercial deals, but with a charge on non-compliant platforms, with every dollar returned to the sector to support journalists.

Other positions included concerns from a speaker who noted 106 local and regional newspapers closed between 2008 and 2018, nearly doubling to 200 since 2019, and worried the code might disadvantage smaller outlets while criticising the government’s undermining of workers’ collective bargaining rights. Independent Senator Rex Patrick’s amendments to address opaque algorithms and big tech business practices were defeated in the Senate on 24 February 2021 by a vote of 12 to 32. Labor also raised concerns about ministerial discretion, potential legal challenges, and a lack of mechanisms to ensure the code increased media diversity or journalist employment, while criticising the Morrison government for not addressing other ACCC recommendations and for lacking transparency on how platform payments were used.

sections.question: What has parliament said about the Screen and Digital Games Industries Bill 2025?
sections.answer:
The Screen and Digital Games Industries Bill 2025 was debated in the New South Wales Parliament, where it received broad cross-party support. The bill repeals the Film and Television Industry Act 1988 and replaces it with a new Act that modernises terminology and includes the digital games industry. It also establishes a Screen and Digital Games Industries Advisory Committee, introduces principles for government agencies and councils to support screen and digital games production, and allows local councils to be accredited as "screen production friendly". The Government said the bill would streamline approvals, reduce red tape and support jobs, noting that New South Wales is home to 22 per cent of Australia's game studios and 16 per cent of its full-time employees in the sector, despite 81 per cent of Australians playing games.

The Opposition supported the bill but moved an amendment, which the Government accepted, to require that at least one member of the advisory committee "have relevant experience in the screen or digital games industry" and "reside or work in regional New South Wales". The Opposition's Kevin Anderson argued that "the regions have been at the very heart of New South Wales filmmaking throughout the industry's history" and raised concerns about regional workers being driven interstate. The Greens also supported the bill and the regional amendment, while calling for broader funding for creatives and diversity on the committee. The Government's John Graham said the bill would help turn New South Wales from a "No State" to a "wholehearted Yes State" for filming, and the bill passed with the amendment agreed to by both houses.

sections.question: What has parliament said about the Music Bill 2026?
sections.answer:
Debate on the Music Bill 2026 in the New South Wales Legislative Council saw The Greens support the bill's intent while arguing it was "welcome, but it is incomplete." Ms Cate Faehrmann, for The Greens, criticised the Government for a "profound contradiction" between its vibrancy claims and police operations that entered queer venues during Pride Month, and for failing to protect the Divine Playhouse venue from eviction. She also argued the bill was wrongly named because it was confined to "contemporary music," excluding classical, jazz and experimental practice, and that it fell short of the Whitlam Government's model of independent cultural institutions. The Greens moved amendments, including to rename the bill, and ultimately commended it to the House.

Minister John Graham, in reply, thanked members and rejected claims the Government stood by over Divine Playhouse, saying it "stands ready to work with the operators to establish a new home." He acknowledged the member's "strong criticisms" and invited her to "back them up with amendments or policy recommendations." On the definition of contemporary music, he said the Government would not support The Greens' definition because it risked excluding country, jazz and blues, but insisted the bill was "absolutely about all music." He conceded her "observations attacking the bill for falling short of the Whitlam benchmark are probably fair." In committee, The Greens amendments Nos 1, 7, 8 and 9 were agreed to, and Ms Faehrmann noted the bill had been renamed the Contemporary Music Bill as a result.

sections.question: What has parliament said about the Sound NSW Advisory Board Bill 2024?
sections.answer:
The Sound NSW Advisory Board Bill 2024 was debated in the New South Wales Parliament, with the bill later passing and being renamed the Sound NSW Advisory Board Bill 2025. The bill sought to legislate the Sound NSW Advisory Board to advise the Minister on the contemporary music industry, formalising an existing non-statutory board. Ms Julia Finn (Labor) moved the bill, noting it would establish the board's composition and functions, and that the Government supported amendments from the Opposition and The Greens, including increasing artist representation to at least two members, defining "artist" inclusively, adding a Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance member, and introducing a review process.

The Hon. John Graham (Labor) said the Government wanted to formalise the board "to make sure that it is there for the long term" and rejected the description of it as "busy work". The Hon. Jacqui Munro (Opposition) supported the bill but moved amendments for at least two artist members and a specific definition of artist, arguing the industry can be "top heavy" and that grassroots members should be represented. Ms Cate Faehrmann (The Greens) supported the bill but moved amendments for greater diversity, including more First Nations and regional representation, a review every three years, and a union member, saying the eligibility criteria "fall short of reflecting the true breadth of the contemporary music industry".

The Hon. Mark Latham criticised the bill as applying "the old, failed doctrines of industry policy" to music, arguing government should not "pick winners" through funding allocations. In reply, Minister Graham acknowledged the challenge of balancing a board "small enough to be able to provide an advisory role in a sensible way" with one "big enough to be diverse", and noted the Government was open to a review function. The bill passed, with the second reading agreed to and the bill read a third time.

sections.question: What has parliament said about SBS headquarters?
sections.answer:
Parliamentary debate on SBS headquarters was sharply partisan. In the Victorian Parliament, Liberal MP Mulholland moved a motion noting SBS is one of two government-funded national broadcasters "both of which are based in Sydney" and that, per the SBS report 2023–24, of 1319 SBS staff "80 per cent were based in New South Wales, while only 14 per cent were based in Victoria." He claimed the Albanese Labor government "forced" the decision to base a new SBS production hub in western Sydney on the SBS board, citing a senior SBS official's evidence at a 12 March 2025 Victorian committee hearing, and condemned the government for "betraying Victoria." He called on the Allan Labor government to advocate for a Melbourne-based SBS headquarters in a multicultural location like Broadmeadows or Dandenong. A Greens MP supported the call for a Melbourne hub, arguing it would mean "local jobs and means local stories," while a Labor MP dismissed the motion as "false outrage," noting the Allan government's investments in Melbourne's west and arguing migrant communities care more about economic development than SBS's location.

In the Commonwealth Parliament, the record is more limited on the headquarters question. In a February 2025 Senate estimates hearing, a senator asked whether "a promise from the previous government that it would look at relocating SBS's headquarters... has come down to a proposal to do a business case on building a production hub in Western Sydney." Separately, Liberal MP Tim James acknowledged SBS's "proud home in Artarmon" and wished it "continued success in Artarmon." Other Commonwealth passages praise SBS as a "national treasure" and defend its funding and impartiality but do not address the headquarters or production hub location.

sections.question: What has parliament said about the Economy and Infrastructure Committee - Inquiry into the Cultural and Creative Industries in Victoria?
sections.answer:
The Victorian Parliament debated the Economy and Infrastructure Committee's inquiry into the cultural and creative industries in Victoria, with several members commenting on its findings. Liberal MP David Davis, who moved a related motion, thanked the committee chair Georgie Purcell and the secretariat for their work, describing it as "a thorough, decent and thoughtful inquiry." He noted the committee reached "some very sensible bipartisan conclusions" but that the Liberals and Nationals put forward a minority report making "a stronger call for more resources in Victoria" and criticising Commonwealth Labor government "interference in the ABC and the SBS" over staffing and head office locations in western Sydney. Another Liberal MP, who spoke on the motion, said they sat on the committee and referenced revelations from its 12 March 2025 public hearing, where a senior SBS official stated the decision to base a new production hub in western Sydney was "forced on SBS by the Albanese Labor government."

A Labor MP who was part of the inquiry responded critically, thanking those who gave evidence but rejecting the Opposition's characterisation of the national broadcasters. They said it was "a little bit rich" for the Opposition to claim the Labor government forced SBS to put staff in western Sydney, given the ABC's funding was "absolutely throttled" under the former Morrison government, and criticised the idea of "telling an organisation what it should do in regard to operational matters." A Greens MP, Georgie Purcell, also thanked the secretariat and creative organisations that contributed, noting the committee was "at its strongest when it recognised and confined its advocacy to getting a better share" of funding, and reiterated the need to protect the ABC and SBS "from political interference in their operational matters." The Greens put forward a minority report proposing measures like a living wage pilot for artists and increased funding for small to medium organisations.

sections.question: What have MPs said about media ownership concentration in Australia since July 2024?
sections.answer:
Several MPs have raised concerns about Australia's concentrated media landscape since July 2024. One member, speaking in the Commonwealth Parliament, said: "Australia already has one of the most concentrated media markets in the developed world," and warned that a new funding mechanism must not "inadvertently make the concentration worse." They noted that independent community, multicultural and regional media organisations—including the Local & Independent News Association, the Community Broadcasting Association of Australia, and the Public Interest Journalism Initiative—have "raised concerns about the potential for the scheme to entrench existing media concentration." Another MP said: "The other problem we have in Australia is a very concentrated media landscape. The big players—News Corp, Nine, Seven West—dominate not just our television screens but the written word, the press and our radio waves," adding that they would "be keeping a very, very close eye on how this scheme rolls out."

A further MP expressed concern that the relevant bills "may not deliver for the small, independent, regional, multicultural and First Nations news organisations" and that they "risk making Australia's media concentration worse rather than better." In a committee estimates hearing, a questioner asked the Australian Communications and Media Authority about "recent media mergers and acquisitions" and what they mean "for media diversity in Australia—namely, the proposed Paramount owned Ten Network's acquisition of WIN assets and the proposed DAZN acquisition of Foxtel." The record also notes that the government "accepts this recommendation in principle" regarding safeguards, though no specific speaker or party is named in that passage. Overall, the record shows bipartisan acknowledgment of concentration as a problem, with particular focus on ensuring any new support scheme does not worsen it.

sections.question: What was said about the news media bargaining code and tech platforms since July 2024?
sections.answer:
Several speakers addressed the news media bargaining code and tech platforms. Coalition speakers claimed credit for the original code and criticised the government's response to Meta's actions. One Coalition speaker said the code "didn't work" because "Tech companies were able to simply opt out of the code by removing news content from their platforms," noting Meta's brief removal of news in 2021 and its April 2024 announcement that it "would not renew commercial deals with Australian news media companies" worth an estimated $70 million a year. Another Coalition speaker called Meta's 2024 decision "pretty disgracefully" and said it "abandoned its obligations, in breach of the law." A third Coalition speaker argued "The problem was never that the code failed. The problem was that the government failed to use it and failed to monitor it," accusing Labor of dismantling the framework rather than amending it.

Government and other speakers defended the new approach. One Labor-aligned speaker said the original code had a weakness: "a platform could remove news from its service and avoid the bargaining obligation," and the new package "strengthens the existing code by addressing that gap." Another speaker noted the code "helped secure commercial agreements" but that "Meta announced that it would not renew its commercial agreements with Australian news companies, which were estimated to be worth around $70 million a year," and platforms could respond to regulation "by removing news from their services altogether." A speaker opposing the bills said the 2021 code's money "went to the three or four biggest incumbents already dominating the market" and that the political establishment "hates" independent platforms and podcasters. The record is limited on this question, with most passages focusing on the code's history and the new incentive scheme rather than detailed post-2024 platform conduct.

sections.question: What has parliament said about Social media age limits?
sections.answer:
Parliamentary debate on social media age limits was sharply divided. The Online Safety Amendment (Social Media Minimum Age) Act 2024 passed Parliament on 29 November 2024, introducing a minimum age of 16 for social media accounts, with the government arguing it protects "young Australians at a critical stage of their development." A government speaker said the law passed "with bipartisan support" and that "Australians should be immensely proud that we are prioritising the online safety of our children and leading the world." Another government-aligned speaker called the ban "one of this parliament's finest moments," crediting parents who had lost children, and noted increased eSafety Commissioner funding and fines of "$49.5 million" for breaches.

Opponents criticised the process and substance. One speaker said the first bill was "rushed through this place in 2024" and "fast-tracked via guillotine," with problems remaining over technology, age assurance, privacy, and the legal test of "reasonable steps." The same speaker claimed the government was "turning a blind eye" to some harms while pursuing others. Another speaker said they "opposed that legislation" in November 2024 because "technological workarounds—VPNs, false age declarations and other methods of circumvention—would inevitably undermine the effectiveness of a blanket ban," citing data confirming those concerns. A Victorian state parliamentarian (Labor) supported a national approach, saying tech companies "see 12- and 14-year-olds as dividends, while we see them as impressionable kids who need to be protected." The eSafety Commissioner confirmed that from 10 December 2025, platforms like Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and X "must deactivate the accounts of children under 16," with "no penalties for social media users" and enforcement focused on "systemic failures by platforms."

eras.label: 1993–2009
eras.question: How did parliament argue about media ownership between 1993 and 2009? The debates of the period included Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Digital Television Switch-over) Bill 2008, Auditor-General’s Reports and Australian Broadcasting Corporation Amendment Bill 2006.
eras.answer:
Debate on media ownership was sharply partisan, with speakers trading accusations about process, broken promises, and the dangers of concentration. A Labor speaker attacked the Howard government for scrapping a promised full public inquiry into cross-media ownership rules, saying the Prime Minister had instead held a "private, in camera departmental review" that produced the recommendation he wanted—to water down or abolish the rules. The speaker claimed this would have let Mr Murdoch buy Channel 7, Mr Packer buy Fairfax, and Channel 10 buy radio stations, and thanked God the Prime Minister was "rolled" on the plan after a public outcry and backbench dissent. The same speaker also criticised the government for stopping an earlier Australian Broadcasting Authority inquiry into a possible fourth commercial television network and for ramming digital television legislation through before an election.

Government and coalition speakers defended reform as necessary modernisation. One coalition speaker said the 2002 bill fulfilled an election commitment and that Australia's media laws, crafted nearly 20 years earlier, were "outmoded" and "seriously hampering" the industry's capacity to meet community needs. Another argued the laws were based on a world without widespread internet, pay TV, or mobile TV, and that the Productivity Commission had found no reason foreign ownership in media should be regulated differently from other industries. They insisted protections remained—the Foreign Acquisitions and Takeovers Act, the Trade Practices Act, and Australian content standards—and that editorial separation requirements would preserve independent voices. A Democrat speaker opposed the 2006 changes, arguing cross-media laws should not change until competition improved, Telstra was divested from Foxtel, and full digitisation was achieved. Labor senators also rejected the 2006 package, saying the government treated the committee process "with contempt" and had done deals at the expense of rural and regional Australia, with one speaker declaring "Shame on the National Party, shame on the Tasmanian Liberal senators."

eras.label: 2010–2019
eras.question: How did parliament argue about media ownership between 2010 and 2019? The debates of the period included Library Amendment Bill 2019 and Committee on Children and Young People.
eras.answer:
Debate on media ownership in this period was framed around the concentration of power and the need for a public interest test. One speaker argued that "the media does fulfil such an important role in civil society; it wields an enormous influence and that power must be wielded responsibly," and pointed to moves by Mr Packer to increase his shareholding in Channel 10 as a reason to revisit "the power of the concentration of media ownership in this country." They insisted that "the concept of a public interest test in relation to control of significant media interests is not a new idea but one that that now must be acted upon in the national interest." Another speaker countered that existing mechanisms already address concentration concerns, saying "we already have a number of mechanisms to address those particular issues. We do not need a public interest arbiter on the top of that particular process."

The debate also involved accusations about process and scrutiny. One opposition member criticised the government for rushing media legislation, comparing it unfavourably to 2006: "In 2006 there were four media bills under consideration. Today there are six bills under consideration. In 2006 the government of the day allowed 34 days for consideration of the bills between the houses. This year, the government of the day is allowing just seven days worth of consideration." They also claimed the government was "behaving as though we are dealing with some minor, non-controversial technical legislation and refusing to allow anything resembling adequate scrutiny of the legislation by this parliament." A government-aligned speaker dismissed such criticism as "hysteria," asserting the reforms were "not an attack on freedom of speech" and that there had been "significant debate in the Australian community for many years, including two significant reviews conducted recently."

The record also notes that new media forms were seen as reducing the stakes of ownership debates. One speaker observed that new forms of publishing—"generally transmitted through the internet, social media, blogs, websites, online newspapers and online discussion forums"—share "mass participation, no single control, self-regulation, easy access and multiple forums," and that there was "no threat to any of those developments." However, a separate speaker cited a 2010 Pew study finding that "96 per cent of stories simply came from recycling stories found in the mainstream press," concluding that "we still rely substantially on traditional news sources" and that people less adept with digital technologies "deserve a diversity of choice just like everyone else." The passages do not name the specific parliaments beyond the Commonwealth, and the record retrieved does not address the Library Amendment Bill 2019 or the Committee on Children and Young People.

eras.label: 2020–2024
eras.question: How did parliament argue about media ownership between 2020 and the middle of 2024? The debates of the period included Defamation (Miscellaneous) Amendment Bill, Regional Media and Regional media.
eras.answer:
Parliamentary debate on media ownership in this period was framed around the decline of regional media and the market power of digital platforms, with speakers repeatedly blaming the government for inaction. In the Commonwealth parliament, Labor speakers, including the member for Gellibrand, argued that the government's 2017 media law changes had failed, claiming they "repealed the two-out-of-three cross-media control rule, which permitted Australia's already highly concentrated media sector to become even more concentrated." Labor's Michelle Rowland, also in the Commonwealth parliament, said the government had left "the hulking analogue framework in place" and had not addressed "the main game around new services, the shift in advertising revenue and the uneven playing field." Centre Alliance's member for Mayo noted that his party, then the Nick Xenophon Team, had in 2017 negotiated for the ACCC inquiry into digital platforms, saying "Google and other platforms have cannibalised local content."

The debates also covered specific bills addressing regional broadcasters. In the Commonwealth parliament, the government's second reading speech for the Broadcasting Services Amendment (Regional Commercial Radio and Other Measures) Bill 2020 said it would ease the regulatory burden on regional commercial radio and television licensees, including by allowing licensees to "self-nominate their own exemption periods" for local content and by inserting a "deeming provision" so regional television licensees could be deemed to have met multichannel Australian content quotas. Labor's shadow minister for communications, Michelle Rowland, criticised the bill as "regulatory housekeeping when major reform is needed," and the member for Gellibrand said it "sells regional Australia short." In the Victorian parliament, the independent member for Shepparton and the opposition's member for Eildon both spoke on the Regulatory Legislation Amendment (Reform) Bill 2021, opposing a provision that would remove the requirement for government notices to be published in print newspapers; the member for Eildon moved amendments to require publication in "a print newspaper circulating in that part of regional or suburban Victoria."

The record also shows debate on whether social media platforms should be treated as publishers. In the Commonwealth parliament, a government statement announced "new powers to force global social media giants to unmask anonymous online trolls," saying "Big tech is now on notice that they will be held to account as publishers of defamation." A notice of motion from Dr Webster called on the government to develop "legislation which holds social media platforms to account as publishers of the content hosted on their sites." However, the record on this specific question is limited: most passages focus on regional media decline and digital platform bargaining power rather than on media ownership concentration itself, and no speaker in the retrieved passages directly debated the merits of ownership limits beyond criticising the 2017 repeal of the cross-media rule.

lede.text:
Parliament argued over the Screen and Digital Games Industries Bill 2025, which passed with cross-party support and a regional advisory-committee amendment, and the Music Bill 2026, where The Greens called it "welcome, but it is incomplete" and Minister Graham conceded criticisms of the Whitlam benchmark were "probably fair."

From 1993 to 2009, Labor attacked Howard's cross-media reforms as backroom deals aiding Murdoch and Packer. In the 2010s, speakers demanded a public interest test against concentrated power. From 2020, debate shifted to regional decline and platform bargaining power. Attention has stayed roughly level across the decades.

A single agreement may account for 25 per cent of total liability; 15 per cent of levy revenue is proposed for grants; Conservatives hold 50 per cent of media's potential audience. Labor supports the bargaining code while wary of concentration; Liberals back the bills but demand genuine commercial outcomes; Independents want fair contributions without favouring the largest companies.
